chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from the one who informed him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

There was a worshipper among the Children of Israel who had not engaged in any worldly affairs. Iblees grunted a grunt, and his army gathered to him. He said, 'Who is for me for that one?' One of them said, 'I am for him.' He said, 'From where he is.' He said, 'From where will you come to him?' He said, 'From the aspect of women.' He said, 'You are not for him; he has not been tested by women.'

Another said to him, 'I am for him.' He said to him, 'From where will you come to him?' He said, 'From the aspect of drink and pleasures.' He said, 'You are not for him; this is not by this.' Another said, 'I am for him.' He said, 'From where will you come to him?' He said, 'From the aspect of righteousness.' He said, 'Go, for you are his master.' So he went to the place of the man and settled near him while he was praying.

He said: And the man used to sleep, and the Devil would not sleep; and he would rest, and the Devil would not rest. So the man turned towards him, and his soul had belittled itself, and he considered his deeds small. So he said, 'O servant of Allah! With what thing have you gained strength for this prayer?' He did not answer him. Then he repeated to him, and he did not answer him. Then he repeated to him again, so he said, 'O servant of Allah! I committed a sin, and I am repentant from it. So whenever I remember the sin, I gain strength for the prayer.'

He said, 'Inform me of your sin so that I may commit it and repent, and if I commit it, I will gain strength for the prayer.' He said, 'Enter the city and ask about so-and-so the prostitute. Give her two dirhams and benefit from her.' He said, 'And from where do I have two dirhams? I do not know what the two dirhams are.' So the Devil took two dirhams from under his foot and handed them to him. So he stood up and entered the city wearing his robes, asking about the house of so-and-so the prostitute. The people guided him, and they thought he had come to advise her, so they guided him.

So he came to her and threw the two dirhams to her and said, 'Stand up.' So she stood up and entered her house, and she said, 'Enter.' And she said, 'You have come to me in a form in which one like me is not visited in such a form. So inform me of your news.' So he informed her. She said to him, 'O servant of Allah! Indeed, leaving the sin is easier than seeking repentance, and not everyone who seeks repentance finds it. And rather, it is befitting that this is a devil who was portrayed for you. So turn away, for you will not see anything.'

So he turned away, and she died that night. When morning came, there was written on her door: 'Attend to so-and-so, for she is from the people of Paradise.' The people became suspicious, so they waited three days and did not bury her due to their doubt in her matter. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to a prophet from the prophets, whom I know only as Musa ibn Imran (peace be upon him): 'Go to so-and-so and pray over her, and order the people to pray over her. For I have forgiven her and obligated Paradise for her, because she discouraged My servant so-and-so from disobeying Me.'
ai.seo_question: How did a devil use a worshipper's humility to lead him into sin, and what was the result?
ai.summary: This narrative from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the subtle danger of *al-hub* (self-deprecation) in Sufi and Shia ascetic traditions, where excessive humility can become a gateway for Iblees to exploit a believer's spiritual vanity. The story highlights the concept of *tathbit* (stabilization), where the prostitute’s act of sending the worshipper away to prevent further sin resulted in her own forgiveness, demonstrating that intent and action in halting sin can be as meritorious as the sin itself. It serves as a cautionary tale against relying on emotional states for spiritual strength rather than consistent devotion.
